title: Optimization of metabolic pathways under stability considerations
contribution: Adds an eigenvalue-based stability constraint to S-system optimization of metabolic networks and solves the resulting bilevel problem, recast as a semi-infinite program, by a global optimization algorithm (abstract).
problem_entry: Steady-state optimization of metabolic networks may return redesigns that are unstable around the new steady state; the paper asks how to guarantee stability (abstract).
key_idea: S-system model plus a matrix-stability (largest eigenvalue) constraint within a prespecified neighbourhood; bilevel problem transformed into a semi-infinite program and solved globally (abstract).
assumptions: Classical S-system representation; stability required within a prespecified neighbourhood of the solution (abstract).
experiments: Tryptophan biosynthesis in bacteria and anaerobic fermentation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (abstract).
limits_future: No limitation stated in the abstract.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: stability as an algebraic constraint, solved globally
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Stability of the redesigned network written as an eigenvalue constraint, giving a bilevel problem solved globally via a semi-infinite reformulation (with S110, S146; S079 in round 1).

transferable: Write dynamic stability as a constraint of the steady-state design problem instead of checking it afterwards, and turn the bilevel result into a semi-infinite program a global method can handle (abstract).

quotes.text: The proposed formulation is a bilevel optimization problem that is very difficult to solve.
We develop a suitable global optimization algorithm to solve this problem after transforming it to a semi-infinite optimization problem.

title: Residue-rotamer-reduction algorithm for the protein side-chain conformation problem
contribution: R3: a global optimization algorithm for protein side-chain conformation that combines residue and rotamer reduction for the first time, simplifying the residue graph and running in 1-10% of the time of the literature MILP approach and 2-78 times faster than SCWRL 3.0 on hard instances (abstract).
problem_entry: Side-chain conformation is central to structure prediction and design, hard in theory, with large realistic instances (abstract).
key_idea: Integrate the two reduction families of the field (residue reduction, rotamer reduction) inside a global optimization algorithm; the reductions simplify the residue graph (abstract).
experiments: 1-10% of the time of the literature MILP approach; 2-78 times faster than SCWRL 3.0 on hard instances (abstract).
positioning: Builds on reduction techniques previously developed for the problem and compares with the MILP approach and SCWRL 3.0 (abstract).
limits_future: Released as an online server (abstract); no limitation stated.

method_links.note: Residue and rotamer reductions shrink the residue graph before the exact search.
A dedicated exact code released as an online server; the abstract does not tie it to BARON.

transferable: Before branching on a combinatorial problem, combine all of the domain's elimination rules, measure how much they shrink the interaction graph, and report speed against both the exact baseline (MILP) and the practitioners' tool (SCWRL) (abstract).

quotes.text: We propose a new global optimization algorithm, which for the first time integrates residue reduction and rotamer reduction techniques previously developed for the protein side-chain conformation problem.
We show that the proposed approach simplifies dramatically the topology of the underlining residue graph.

title: A branch-and-reduce algorithm for the contact map overlap problem
contribution: A branch-and-reduce exact algorithm for contact map overlap that works on the native problem with structure-based bounds and reductions; faster than the best previous algorithms on more than 36,000 literature instances, with clusters matching SCOP (abstract).
problem_entry: CMO is a reliable fold-similarity measure whose clusterings agree with experts, but it is NP-hard and few exact algorithms exist (abstract).
key_idea: Branch-and-reduce on CMO in its natural form, with bounding and reduction procedures from the problem structure, instead of transforming it to another combinatorial problem (abstract).
experiments: Over 36,000 literature test problems; significantly faster and solves many more challenging test sets than the best previous algorithms; clusters agree with SCOP (abstract).
positioning: Contrasts itself with previous exact approaches that transform CMO into other combinatorial problems (abstract).
limits_future: No limitation stated in the abstract; RECOMB 2006 acceptance rate 18.5% (CV §IV.B2 item 5; metadata).

method_links.note: Branch-and-reduce (structure-based bounding and reduction) carried to a protein-structure problem; SKILL Method 1 already cites this DOI.
Own exact method judged against the best previous exact algorithms on more than 36,000 literature instances and against the SCOP expert classification; not a benchmark-first study.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Solves CMO in its natural form rather than after transformation to another combinatorial problem (with S071, S197).

transferable: Keep the problem in its native formulation and derive bounds and domain reductions from its structure instead of translating it for an off-the-shelf solver; validate on literature instances and on the application's own ground truth (here SCOP) (abstract).

quotes.text: Contrary to previous approaches, we do not transform CMO to other combinatorial optimization problems for solution.
By exploiting the problem’s mathematical structure, we develop bounding and reduction procedures that lead to a very efficient algorithm.

title: A reduction-based exact algorithm for the contact map overlap problem
contribution: Journal version of the reduction-based exact CMO algorithm (structure-based lower and upper bounding and reduction), faster than existing exact methods and solving previously unsolved hard instances, with an on-line server (abstract).
problem_entry: Structural alignment for classification, database search, function prediction and fold-prediction assessment, via CMO maximization (abstract).
key_idea: Solve CMO directly, not after transformation, with structure-based lower bounding, upper bounding and reduction schemes (abstract).
experiments: Significantly faster than existing exact algorithms; some hard instances solved for the first time; clusters agree with SCOP (abstract).
positioning: Against exact methods that transform CMO into other combinatorial problems (abstract).
writing: Journal counterpart of S126 (inferred from title, authors and the matching abstracts).

method_links.note: Reduction schemes at the centre of an exact algorithm.
A dedicated on-line server rather than a module of the production solver.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Solves CMO directly rather than after transformation (with S126, S197).

quotes.text: We exploit the mathematical structure of the problem in order to develop a number of efficient lower bounding, upper bounding, and reduction schemes.
Computational experiments demonstrate that our algorithm runs significantly faster than existing exact algorithms and solves some hard CMO instances that were not solved in the past.

title: Global optimization in stabilizing controller design
contribution: Recasts stabilizing controller design as bilevel programs, reduces them via the Hurwitz conditions to single-level nonconvex programs solved by branch-and-reduce, and raises the Belgian chocolate stabilizability lower bound from 0.96 to 0.973974 (abstract).
problem_entry: Feedback stabilization problems from the literature, including the Belgian chocolate problem (abstract).
key_idea: Bilevel formulation, Hurwitz conditions to obtain an equivalent single-level nonconvex program, branch-and-reduce global solution (abstract).
proof_devices: equivalent single-level reformulation via the Hurwitz stability conditions (abstract)
experiments: Improved solutions for two literature problems; Belgian chocolate lower bound raised from 0.96 to 0.973974 (abstract).
limits_future: Listed on the BARON publications page among works that describe BARON, its methodology and applications (metadata); minlp.org library entry S204.

method_links.note: The production branch-and-reduce algorithm is the engine for a new application class (controller design).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: stability as an algebraic constraint, solved globally
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Stabilization written through Hurwitz inequalities as a single-level nonconvex program and solved globally (with S078, S146).

transferable: Replace a stability requirement by finitely many algebraic Hurwitz inequalities so that the design becomes a single-level nonconvex program a global solver can attack (abstract).

quotes.text: By invoking the Hurwitz stability conditions, we reformulate these bilevel programs to equivalent single-level nonconvex optimization programs.
In addition, we improve the lower bound of the stabilizability parameter of the Belgian chocolate problem from the previous best known 0.96 to 0.973974.

title: An integer minimal principle and triplet sieve method for phasing centrosymmetric structures
contribution: An integer minimal principle model for centrosymmetric phasing that handles the phase shifts of non-symmorphic space groups, a characterization of its false minima by even and odd triplets, and a triplet sieve (elimination on reliable triplets, enumeration of the remaining freedom, expansion in SnB) (abstract).
problem_entry: The integer minimal principle for centrosymmetric structures must account for reciprocal-space phase shifts of non-symmorphic space groups (abstract).
key_idea: Characterize false minima via even and odd triplets; Gaussian elimination on reliable triplet subsets from progressively smaller sets of strongest reflections; enumerate the degrees of freedom; expand in SnB; pick by two figures of merit (abstract).
proof_devices: characterization of false minima in terms of even and odd triplets (abstract)
experiments: Computational results for a variety of structures (abstract).
limits_future: The sieve later went into SnB 2.3 (S161).

method_links.note: Weak: a cheap exact inference (elimination on reliable triplets) settles the phases up to the remaining degrees of freedom before anything is enumerated.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Several phase solution sets are generated by enumerating the degrees of freedom and screened by figures of merit (with S174).

transferable: Find out why the model has spurious minima and design the search to avoid them; run the fast exact step on the most reliable data only and enumerate just the degrees of freedom it leaves open (abstract).
coauthors: A. B. Smith (first author), H. Xu

quotes.text: Additionally, characterization of false minima of the model is done in terms of even and odd triplets.
First, Gaussian elimination using only a subset of reliable triplets is employed for phasing.

title: A branch-and-bound algorithm for the continuous facility layout problem
contribution: Proves that finitely many candidate layouts suffice for the continuous facility layout problem and builds on it a specialized branch-and-bound that outperforms three existing approaches (abstract).
problem_entry: Continuous facility layout models fix the limits of earlier models but are solvable to optimality only for tiny instances (abstract).
key_idea: Finiteness theorem (finitely many candidate solutions suffice) plus a structure-exploiting branch-and-bound that prunes large parts of the space (abstract).
proof_devices: finiteness theorem: enumerating finitely many candidate layouts secures an optimum (abstract)
limits_future: Extensions to more general layout instances discussed (abstract).

method_links.note: The search space is cut once, by a finiteness theorem and structural pruning, rather than by node-wise range reduction.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A continuous problem with infinitely many feasible layouts reduced to finitely many candidates (with S354; S014 in round 1).

transferable: Before writing a branch-and-bound for a continuous geometric problem, look for a theorem that an optimum lies among finitely many combinatorial configurations, then search over those (abstract).

quotes.text: We prove that it suffices to enumerate finitely many candidate solutions to secure an optimal solution, despite the fact that CFL admits infinitely many feasible layouts.
Comprehensive computational studies show that this new algorithm substantially outperforms three existing approaches.

title: Finite Algorithms for Global Minimization of Separable Concave Programs
contribution: Reviews elements of four finite algorithms for minimizing separable concave functions over a polytope as illustrations of how algorithmic constructs let continuous branch-and-bound terminate finitely (abstract).
problem_entry: Branch-and-bound on continuous global optimization is an infinite process whose bounds need not meet in finitely many iterations (abstract).
key_idea: Review four finite, non-exhaustive algorithms for separable concave minimization over a polytope, a class with a naive finite algorithm (abstract).
writing: Uses the class as a teaching case for algorithmic constructs in continuous global optimization (abstract).
limits_future: Which four algorithms are reviewed is not stated in the abstract; chapter from the Fields workshop of May 2007 (AMS contents page).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Finite algorithms for separable concave programs as remedies for the infinite nature of continuous branch-and-bound (with S047; S014 in round 1).

transferable: Use a problem class where finite termination is attainable as a laboratory for isolating which constructs make continuous branch-and-bound finish (abstract).
coauthors: X. Bao (first author per Crossref, zbMATH, AMS and the CV; works.json lists Sahinidis alone)

quotes.text: When applied to continuous global optimization problems, branch-and-bound algorithms are infinite processes, in the sense that the lower and upper bounds they provide converge but not necessarily become equal in a finite number of iterations.

Even though a naive finite algorithm exists for this class of global optimization problems, the algorithms addressed here are not exhaustive and illustrate how certain algorithmic constructs serve to overcome some of the challenges in continuous global optimization.

title: GPU computing with Kaczmarz's and other iterative algorithms for linear systems
contribution: Compares GPU and CPU implementations of six iterative linear solvers on convection-dominated PDE systems; the GPU versions win, and the out-of-favour CGNR performs best on the GPU (abstract).
problem_entry: Large linear systems from strongly convection-dominated PDEs on a GPU (abstract).
key_idea: Compare Kaczmarz, Cimmino, component averaging, CGNR, SSOR-PCG and CARP-CG on GPU and CPU, for dense and banded systems (abstract).
experiments: GPU beats CPU and earlier cluster and shared-memory implementations; CGNR best on the GPU, ahead of a cluster CARP-CG (abstract).
positioning: Revisits CGNR, which had fallen out of favour for such problems (abstract).
limits_future: An empirical comparison, not a new method; open NIH author manuscript PMC2879082 not read here.

method_links.note: Benchmark-first entry into a new area (GPU linear algebra) comparing existing methods rather than proposing one; no certified ground truth or portfolio in the abstract.

coauthors: J. M. Elble (first author), P. Vouzis

quotes.text: The results demonstrate that our GPU implementation outperforms CPU implementations of these algorithms, as well as previously studied parallel implementations on Linux clusters and shared memory systems.

While the CGNR method had begun to fall out of favor for solving such problems, for the problems studied in this paper, the CGNR method implemented on the GPU performed better than the other methods, including a cluster implementation of the CARP-CG method.

title: Portfolio optimization for wealth-dependent risk preferences
contribution: Models wealth-dependent risk attitudes by an indefinite quadratic utility around a goal over return scenarios and solves the nonconvex portfolio problem globally, giving higher-skewness portfolios than mean-variance (abstract).
problem_entry: Utility is typically multimodal: risk-averse at some wealth levels, risk-seeking at others (abstract).
key_idea: Indefinite quadratic utility with convex and concave segments around a fixed goal; scenario returns; global optimization of the nonconvex problem (abstract).
assumptions: Uncertainty as a finite set of return scenarios (abstract).
experiments: Effect of short sales; systematically higher skewness than expectation-variance portfolios (abstract).
positioning: Departs from the classical expectation-variance approach (abstract).
limits_future: Listed on the BARON publications page (metadata).
transferable: Replace a convenient convex modelling assumption (concave utility) by the empirically supported nonconvex one and let a global solver carry the nonconvexity (abstract).

quotes.text: In this paper, we consider the problem of optimizing the portfolio of an investor with an indefinite quadratic utility function.

We present computational results which investigate the effect of short sales and demonstrate that the proposed approach systematically produces portfolios with higher values of skewness than the classical expectation-variance approach.

title: Synthesis of optimal adsorptive carbon capture processes.
contribution: Presentation abstract: a superstructure framework for solid-sorbent carbon capture synthesis that replaces intractable Aspen Custom Modeler reactor models by simple algebraic surrogates (abstract).
problem_entry: CCSI needs superstructure-based synthesis of a solid-sorbent capture process, but the detailed reactor models are intractable inside optimization (abstract).
key_idea: Generate simple algebraic surrogate models of the reactor models and use them in a superstructure formulation choosing among reactor types and configurations (abstract).
limits_future: The presentation describes the formulation and the resulting optimal configuration; no numbers in the abstract.

method_links.note: Simulator-only reactor models replaced by simple algebraic surrogates so that synthesis can be optimized; earliest instance in this batch (2010).

coauthors: A. Cozad (first author), H. Kim, A. Lee, P. Vouzis, M. Konda, A. Simon and others

quotes.text: Detailed process models for these reactors have been modeled using Aspen Custom Modeler; however, such models are computationally intractable for large optimization-based process synthesis.

Thus, in order to facilitate the use of these models for process synthesis, we have developed an approach for generating simple algebraic surrogate models that can be used in an optimization formulation.

title: Novel Relaxations for Global Optimization
contribution: NSF award abstract (2010): plans closed-form convex and concave envelopes of nonconvex functions that minimize or remove factorable decomposition, to be tested in branch-and-cut for NLP and MINLP (abstract).
problem_entry: Global solvers exist but vast classes of applications remain out of reach; sharp relaxations are the heart of the problem (abstract).
key_idea: Closed-form envelopes from convex analysis replacing much of the factorable decomposition; analytical envelopes for functions from many applications; computational study in branch-and-cut (abstract).
positioning: Factorable programming is easy to automate but often weak (abstract).
limits_future: A funded plan; results not part of the abstract. Compare S109 (round 1).

method_links.note: The stated goal is sharper relaxations, with their computational implications in branch-and-cut a follow-up task, rather than bound per second as the deciding criterion.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: envelopes of whole functions instead of factorable decomposition
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Plan to derive convex and concave envelopes of whole nonconvex functions in closed form, minimizing or eliminating factorable decomposition.

quotes.text: The primary goal of this project is to address the problem that lies at the heart of global optimization algorithms, i.e., the construction of sharp relaxations.
While it is easy to automate, this factorable programming technique often leads to weak relaxations.

limits_future: Listed on the BARON publications page (metadata).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: stability as an algebraic constraint, solved globally

quotes.text: The underlying mathematical problem is difficult to solve as it involves infinitely many constraints, nonconvexities and multiple local optima.
We propose a successive row and column generation algorithm to solve the resulting generalized semi‐infinite programming problem to global optimality.

title: Optimization of imc-pid tuning parameters for adaptive control: part 1

title: An integer programming approach to DNA sequence assembly
contribution: An integer programming and global optimization approach to DNA sequence assembly with data errors that certifies optimality for sequences over 10,000 long and enumerates all alternative reconstructions (abstract).
problem_entry: With errors, de novo assembly is hard and need not have a unique reconstruction; heuristics overlook the alternatives (abstract).
key_idea: Integer programming formulation, global optimization solution strategy, and a technique to identify all alternative reconstructs (abstract).
experiments: Sequencing-by-hybridization examples: over 10,000 length with a global optimality certificate, more than 10 times longer than before; alternatives differ widely in reproducing the target (abstract).
positioning: Against heuristic approaches that overlook alternative solutions (abstract).
limits_future: Alternative solutions to refine results and guide further experiments (abstract).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: All alternative optimal reconstructions are enumerated and compared (with S184; S035 in round 1).

transferable: After solving to global optimality, enumerate all alternative optima and report how much they differ on the quantity the user cares about; use the spread to choose the next experiment (abstract).

quotes.text: The enumeration of all alternative solutions is important in drawing a reliable conclusion on the target sequence, and is often overlooked in the heuristic approaches that are currently available.

When applied to examples of sequencing-by-hybridization, our approach dramatically increases the length of DNA sequences that can be handled with global optimality certificate to over 10,000, which is more than 10 times longer than previously reported.
